title: Eben Sadie and the Swartland Revolution
dek: How a winemaker with eight thousand pounds and a stubborn vision turned a forgotten wheat belt into South Africa's most talked-about wine region.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: The Wheat Country Nobody Wanted

Drive an hour north of Cape Town, past the satellite towns of the Northern Suburbs, and the landscape changes. Vineyards give way to wheat fields. The air turns dry, the light sharpens, and the rolling hills of the Swartland stretch toward a horizon that seems borrowed from a different country. For most of the twentieth century, this was not where South African fine wine was supposed to come from. The Swartland was the bulk basket, the place cooperatives sent tankers to collect grapes by the tonne. Then Eben Sadie arrived.

Sadie founded The Sadie Family Wines in 1999, capitalised with roughly the equivalent of eight thousand pounds. It was, by any measure, an act of faith. He had trained in Germany and Austria, worked vintages across Europe, and returned to the Western Cape convinced that the Swartland's old, dry-farmed bush vines were not a relic to be grubbed up but a treasure hiding in plain sight. The region's schist, granite, and iron-rich soils, combined with brutal summers and cooling afternoon winds from the Atlantic, reminded him of the Rhône. He bet everything on the comparison.
Columella and the Birth of a Cult

The first vintage of Columella, Sadie's flagship red, was the 2000 vintage — just seventeen barrels, around five thousand bottles, a Syrah-led blend that also drew on old-vine Mourvèdre, Grenache, Tinta Barroca, and Carignan. The grapes came from eight scattered vineyards across the Swartland, each chosen for its soil and aspect. There was no estate, no visitors' centre, no marketing department. There was a man, a rented cellar, and a conviction that South Africa could make a red blend to stand with anything in the world.

Columella arrived like a hand grenade in the local wine scene. Critics who had written off South African reds as either overripe fruit bombs or thin, herbaceous efforts suddenly had to recalibrate. Here was a wine of structure and tension, savoury and deeply mineral, with none of the sweetness that defined so much of the country's output. Within a few vintages it was being called South Africa's finest red, and Sadie — intense, opinionated, allergic to compromise — was being described as the enfant terrible of Cape wine, and occasionally as the country's first rockstar winemaker.
Palladius and the White That Changed Everything

If Columella proved the Swartland could do serious red, Palladius proved it could do white. A blend of eleven varieties — Chenin Blanc at its core, supported by Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Viognier, Verdelho, Marsanne, Roussanne, Semillon Gris, and others — drawn from seventeen vineyards, Palladius is a wine that defies easy description. It is rich yet grippy, broad yet saline, a white wine with the spine of a great red. The 2023 vintage drew a near-perfect score from James Suckling, who named the Swartland as the region 'pointing the way' for all of South African wine.
Columella changes every ten years. The blend, the vineyards, the way it ages — it is a living thing, not a recipe.

Sadie now farms his own land, including the Rotsvas parcel near Malmesbury, and continues to source from some of the oldest vineyards in the region. The cellar is still deliberately small. Production is measured in thousands of bottles, not millions. And yet the influence is out of all proportion to the scale. Every ambitious young winemaker who has moved to the Swartland in the past two decades — and there have been dozens — is, in some sense, working in the landscape Eben Sadie opened up. He did not invent the Swartland. He simply insisted that the world look at it properly.

title: Andrea Mullineux: The Swartland's Californian Voice
dek: A first-generation winemaker from California fell in love with a South African, a region, and a grape — and helped define what Swartland Syrah can be.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: Two First-Generation Winemakers

Chris Mullineux is South African. His wife Andrea is Californian. Neither grew up in wine; both came to it through study, travel, and a willingness to start at the bottom. They met in the Swartland in the mid-2000s, when the region's revolution was still in its first flush, and they founded Mullineux Family Wines in 2007 with a narrow ambition: to make wines that told the truth about a place.

The place they chose was not Stellenbosch, the obvious answer, but the Swartland — dry, hot, worked for generations by cooperatives, and at that moment the most exciting frontier in South African wine. Andrea, who had studied viticulture and enology at UC Davis and worked harvests in Napa, Sonoma, and Stellenbosch, found in the Swartland's schist and granite hills something she had not found anywhere else: vineyards old enough, and poor enough, to force the vines to speak.
The Syrah That Made the Name

Of all the Mullineux wines, it is the Syrah that first drew international attention. The flagship is the Trifecta Syrah, sourced from three of the Swartland's top vineyard sites — one on schist, one on granite, one on iron-rich soils. The idea is simple and obsessive: let each soil type express itself through the same grape, then blend them into something that is somehow more than the sum. The result is a Syrah of startling freshness in a warm climate — peppery, dark-fruited, with a savory edge that has drawn comparisons to the Northern Rhône.
The Swartland forces honesty. You cannot hide behind irrigation, behind new oak, behind extraction. The vineyards either have something to say or they don't.

Andrea's reputation has grown steadily. She has been named Winemaker of the Year by the Platter's South African Wine Guide — a rare honor for anyone, and a milestone for a woman in an industry still dominated by men. The winery, now part of the Mullineux & Leeu Family Wines group with a second property in Franschhoek, produces a small portfolio: Syrah in several iterations, old-vine Chenin Blanc under the Kloof Street and Straw Wine labels, and a handful of single-vineyard whites that have become reference points for what the Swartland can do.
Great Heart and the Question of Ownership

In recent years, the Mullineuxs have also built Great Heart Wines, a project that is one hundred percent owned by the people who make the wine — the farm workers and cellar staff. It is a quiet act of transformation in an industry still grappling with its apartheid legacy, and it reflects the same instinct that drew Andrea to the Swartland in the first place: the belief that good wine and good practice are not separate questions.

Andrea's influence extends well beyond her own bottles. She has become a mentor to a younger generation of winemakers — particularly women — entering a profession that, in South Africa as everywhere, has historically been dominated by men. She speaks openly about the early years, when she was the only woman in many a cellar and tasting room, and about the slow, stubborn work of building credibility in a culture that did not always offer it freely. Her response, characteristically, was to make better wine than anyone who doubted her. The Swartland that nobody wanted has become the region everyone watches, and Andrea Mullineux is one of the central reasons why — a Californian who saw, in a dry corner of the Western Cape, the possibility of a wine culture that could stand alongside any in the world.

title: Ntsiki Biyela: South Africa's First Black Woman Winemaker
dek: From a village in KwaZulu-Natal to the cellar floor — the story of a pioneer who changed what a South African winemaker is allowed to look like.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: Mahlabathini to Stellenbosch

Ntsiki Biyela grew up in Mahlabathini, a village in the hills of KwaZulu-Natal, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest vineyard. Wine was not part of her world. She had never tasted it. She did not know anyone who made it. Then, in the late 1990s, she was awarded a bursary from South African Airways to study winemaking at Stellenbosch University — a programme aimed at opening the wine industry to black South Africans who had been systematically excluded from it for generations.

She arrived at Stellenbosch as the only black woman in her class, in a town where the wine culture was overwhelmingly white and Afrikaans, and where the cellar was still, in many cases, a place where black hands did the work and white faces made the decisions. She graduated with a BSc in Oenology and, in 2004, took up her first winemaking role at Stellekaya — becoming, quietly and irreversibly, the first black woman to work as a winemaker in South Africa.
Learning to Speak in Wine

At Stellekaya, Biyela spent thirteen years making wine, learning the craft, and — in her telling — learning to translate. She had grown up speaking Zulu, studying in English, and working in Afrikaans. Wine, she realised, was another language, and she set herself the task of mastering it. Her red blends earned medals at national competitions. International critics began to take note. But the more she learned, the more she felt the pull of something that was entirely her own.
I had to learn so many languages. Zulu, English, Afrikaans. And then there was wine. Wine was the hardest, because no one expects you to speak it.

In 2016, she left Stellekaya and founded Aslina Wines, naming the brand after her late grandmother, Aslina, who had raised her and whose strength she credits as the foundation of everything she has built. The name is deliberate. Biyela's story is often told as a story of firsts — first black woman winemaker, first this, first that — but the name Aslina points somewhere else: to the women, the grandmothers, the generations who never had the chance and whose labor made hers possible.
A Brand That Travels

Aslina's portfolio — a Sauvignon Blanc, a Cabernet Sauvignon, a Chardonnay, and a Bordeaux-style red blend called Umthunzi — now appears on lists in the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond. The Cabernet, in particular, has drawn notice: a Stellenbosch fruit-forward style with cassis, blackberry, and plum, but with a structure and restraint that signals a winemaker in full command of her voice. Biyela has been profiled by Forbes, interviewed by Grape Collective, and featured in documentaries about the changing face of South African wine.

What makes Biyela's story resonate beyond the cellar is that she has never framed it as exceptional. She speaks, instead, about the thousands of black South Africans who grew up in wine country and were never allowed to taste what they helped produce. Her presence on an international stage is not just a personal triumph. It is a reminder of how much talent the industry left on the table for three centuries — and how much it has to gain by opening its doors.

title: Marc Kent and The Chocolate Block
dek: How a maverick winemaker turned a Syrah-led blend into one of South Africa's most successful — and most imitated — wines.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: Seven Friends and a Farm in Franschhoek

Boekenhoutskloof was founded in 1993 by six friends, among them the late Tim Rands of the Vinimark distribution group. The farm sits in a narrow valley outside Franschhoek, a region better known then for white wine and hospitality than for serious reds. Marc Kent, a young winemaker with a reputation for doing things his own way, joined as the seventh shareholder in December 1994. He has been the technical director and the driving creative force behind the estate ever since.

The early vintages were modest in volume and ambition. Kent made a Semillon from old Franschhoek vines, a Syrah, a Cabernet Sauvignon. The wines were good, even impressive, but they were not yet the phenomenon that would define the estate. That phenomenon was still to come, and it would arrive with a name that sounded more like a confection than a wine: The Chocolate Block.
A Blend Born from a Conversation

The origin story of The Chocolate Block involves the UK high-street retailer Oddbins, which in the early 2000s was looking for a distinctive South African red to sell to British drinkers. Kent, who had been experimenting with a Rhône-style blend built on Syrah with support from Grenache, Cinsault, and a splash of Viognier, produced a wine that was plush, approachable, and unmistakably serious. The name came in part from the wine's brooding, cocoa-adjacent character — the savoury, dark-fruited depth that old-vine Swartland Syrah can deliver — and in part from sheer marketing instinct.
I wanted to make a wine that people could drink on a Tuesday and age for a decade. That's the tension that makes it interesting.

The Chocolate Block launched in the early 2000s and grew with startling speed. By the late 2010s it had reached roughly 740,000 bottles a year — a volume almost unheard of for a wine at that quality and price point. It became, as one UK trade publication put it, 'one of South Africa's greatest winemaking stories,' not because it was the most rarefied wine in the country, but because it proved that a meticulously made blend could find a mass audience without dumbing itself down.
Beyond the Block

Kent has not let The Chocolate Block define him entirely. The estate's flagship Syrah, sourced from Swartland vineyards rather than Franschhoek, remains a reference point for the grape in South Africa. The Semillon, drawn from vines planted in 1902, 1936, and 1942, is one of the most lauded old-vine whites in the country. And Kent has been an outspoken advocate for the broader Swartland movement, buying fruit from the region's old-vine growers and helping to build the market that sustains them.

What sets Kent apart is a refusal to choose between accessibility and ambition. He is a maverick in the sense that matters: not someone who breaks rules for the sake of it, but someone who quietly insists that the rules be re-examined in light of what the land and the market actually allow. The Chocolate Block is the proof. It sells in numbers that would have been unthinkable for a South African blend a generation ago, and it sells because it is good — a sentence that should not need writing, but in the context of South African wine history, still does.

title: Vin de Constance: Napoleon's Deathbed Wine
dek: The legendary sweet wine of Constantia — beloved by emperors and novelists, lost for a century, and reborn on the slopes of Table Mountain.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: The Garden at the End of Africa

In 1685, Simon van der Stel, Governor of the Cape of Good Hope, was granted a tract of land on the lower slopes of Table Mountain. He named it Constantia, and he planted vines. The choice of site was no accident: the Constantia valley sits close to the cold Atlantic, fanned by south-easterly winds, with decomposed granite soils that drain quickly and force the vines to work. Van der Stel's ambition was to make wine that could stand alongside Europe's best. Within a generation, his successors had done something stranger: they had made a wine that Europe could not match.

That wine was Constantia — later known as Vin de Constance — a natural sweet wine made from Muscat de Frontignan grapes left to ripen and partially raisin on the vine. It was not fortified. Its sweetness came from the fruit itself, concentrated by the Cape sun and the cooling sea breezes that slowed the ripening. By the late eighteenth century, it was one of the most famous wines in the world.
The Emperor's Daily Comfort

The most enduring legend of Vin de Constance concerns Napoleon Bonaparte. Exiled to Saint Helena in 1815, the deposed emperor is said to have requested a glass of the wine on his deathbed in 1821. Whether the story is literally true in its final detail, the broader record is clear: throughout his exile, Napoleon ordered Constance wine regularly, sometimes as many as thirty bottles at a time. It was his daily comfort, smuggled past his British jailers, the last pleasure of a man who had once ruled the continent.

Napoleon was far from alone. Frederick the Great of Prussia was a devotee. King George IV of England kept it in his cellars. Lord Nelson drank it at sea. Jane Austen referenced it in her unfinished novel The Mystery of Edwin Drood, and Charles Baudelaire praised it in verse. For a century, Vin de Constance was the sweet wine against which all others were measured — a symbol not just of South African winemaking, but of luxury itself.
A Century of Silence

Then, in the late nineteenth century, it vanished. Phylloxera reached the Cape. The estate that produced the wine was subdivided and sold. The vineyards were replanted to other varieties, or abandoned entirely. For nearly a hundred years, Vin de Constance existed only in literature and in the memories of old European cellars. The wine that Napoleon drank was, apparently, gone forever.

It was not. In the 1980s, the Klein Constantia estate — one of the fragments of the original Constantia farm — began a project to recreate the wine. Cuttings of Muscat de Frontignan were sourced. The original vineyard sites were replanted. Winemakers pored over nineteenth-century records to reconstruct the method: late harvest, natural sweetness, slow fermentation, ageing in old oak. The maiden vintage of the revived Vin de Constance was 1986. It was, by all accounts, a near-miraculous act of resurrection.
A Legend, Back in the Bottle

Today, Vin de Constance is once again one of the most sought-after sweet wines in the world. It is made in small quantities from a single vineyard on the slopes of Table Mountain, aged for several years in a combination of French oak and stainless steel, and released only when the estate believes it is ready. Critics have awarded it some of the highest scores ever given to a South African wine. The wine that Napoleon drank on Saint Helena is, against all odds, drinkable again — and it tastes, by every account, exactly as it should: of honey and apricot and orange peel, of the sea wind off the Cape, and of a history that refused to end.

title: Kanonkop and the Invention of Pinotage
dek: The Stellenbosch estate that took South Africa's only native grape from curiosity to icon — and the winemaker who put it on the world map.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Grape Born in a Lab

Pinotage is South Africa's only truly native wine grape, and it was born not in a vineyard but in a laboratory. In 1925, Professor Abraham Perold, the first professor of viticulture at Stellenbosch University, crossed Pinot Noir and Cinsaut — then known in South Africa as Hermitage — and planted the four resulting seedlings in his garden. The cross was an attempt to combine the elegance of Pinot Noir with the hardiness of Cinsaut. The result, for decades, was a grape that nobody quite knew what to do with.

The first Pinotage wine was made in 1941 at Elsenburg Agricultural College. Early efforts were mixed. The grape could produce vivid, fruity wines, but it could also produce something paint-like and harsh, and for years it was treated as a curiosity at best, a fault at worst. Then came Kanonkop, the Stellenbosch estate that had planted Pinotage in the 1940s on the lower slopes of the Simonsberg, and that would, over the second half of the twentieth century, do more than any other producer to define what the grape could be.
1973 and the First Estate Vintage

Kanonkop released its first wine under the Kanonkop brand in 1973, and from that first estate vintage, Pinotage was the focal point. The estate's old bush vines, planted in decomposed granite soils and farmed without irrigation, produced fruit of a density and concentration that earlier winemakers had never accessed. The Pinotage was aged in French oak, treated with the seriousness usually reserved for Cabernet, and released only after extended time in bottle.

The turning point came with Beyers Truter. Truter started working with Kanonkop in the late 1980s and developed a winemaking technique — involving careful temperature control, shorter maceration, and the avoidance of the over-extraction that had plagued earlier Pinotages — that transformed the grape's reputation. His 1989 Kanonkop Pinotage, the first vintage using the new approach, won the Robert Mondavi Trophy at the 1991 International Wine and Spirit Competition. For the first time, a Pinotage had beaten the world's best reds on a global stage.
Pinotage is not a difficult grape. It is a grape that demands respect. If you rush it, it will punish you. If you listen to it, it will reward you.
The Paul Sauer and the Pinotage Association

Alongside the Pinotage, Kanonkop makes the Paul Sauer — a Bordeaux-style blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Cabernet Franc, first produced in 1981 and named after the farm's patriarch — which has become, in the eyes of many critics, South Africa's finest red wine. Truter, who became synonymous with Kanonkop before leaving to found his own estate, also established the Pinotage Association in 1995, an industry body dedicated to improving the quality and reputation of the grape.

Today, Kanonkop remains family-owned, run by the Sauer and Krige families, and its Pinotage — from vines some of which are over seventy years old — is still the benchmark against which all other South African Pinotages are measured. The grape that was once a national embarrassment is now, thanks largely to this one estate, a point of pride. It is a reminder that native does not mean second-rate, and that a single producer, patient enough and stubborn enough, can change what a whole country believes about itself.

title: Hamilton Russell and the Hemel-en-Aarde Bet
dek: How Anthony Hamilton Russell proved that South Africa could make world-class Pinot Noir — by planting it where nobody thought it would grow.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Valley Between the Mountains and the Sea

The Hemel-en-Aarde valley runs from the outskirts of Hermanus toward the Atlantic coast, a narrow corridor of low hills and cold air squeezed between the Onrust Mountains and the sea. The name, in Afrikaans, means 'Heaven and Earth,' and for most of the twentieth century it was known for little more than its scenery and its whales. Wine, in the South African imagination, came from Stellenbosch and Franschhoek, not from a wind-scoured valley near Walker Bay. Anthony Hamilton Russell set out to change that.

The estate had been founded by his father, Tim Hamilton Russell, in 1975, on the hunch that the valley's cool climate — cooled by cold Benguela-current air funnelling in from the ocean — might be suitable for varieties that South Africa had previously struggled with. When Anthony took over in the early 1990s, he narrowed the focus. He bet the estate on two grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. It was, at the time, an act of near-reckless conviction.
Proving Pinot in Africa

Pinot Noir is the most demanding of grapes. It ripens late, rots easily, and punishes any site that is too warm, too fertile, or too exposed. For decades, the consensus in the international wine world was that South Africa was simply too hot to make serious Pinot. Hamilton Russell, working with low-vigour stony soils, careful clonal selection, and the natural refrigeration of the Hemel-en-Aarde, set out to test the consensus.

The early vintages were promising. The wines had a purity and a structure that South African Pinot had rarely shown. By the 2000s, Hamilton Russell Pinot Noir was being taken seriously in Burgundy itself — no small feat for a producer from a region that, a decade earlier, most French winemakers would not have been able to locate on a map. The wine is aged in French oak from François Frères, made in small quantities, and built for the table rather than the tasting competition: spicy, savoury, with plum and black-cherry fruit and a ferrous grip that speaks to the clay-rich soils.
An Appellation Reimagined

Anthony Hamilton Russell's influence extends beyond his own bottles. He was instrumental in the subdivision of the Wine of Origin Hemel-en-Aarde region into three distinct appellations — the Valley, the Ridge, and the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde — each defined by specific soil and climatic conditions. The Ridge appellation was created in 2009, recognising that the higher, cooler sites produced wines distinct enough to warrant their own designation. It was an act of terroir-mindedness almost unprecedented in South African wine regulation.

Today, the Hemel-en-Aarde is dotted with producers — Crystallum, Creation, Bouchard Finlayson, Gottfried Mocke, and others — making some of the country's most exciting Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. They all owe something to the Hamilton Russell bet. Anthony Hamilton Russell proved, against the prevailing wisdom, that South Africa could make Burgundian varieties with grace and age-worthiness — and in doing so, he opened a corner of the Cape that is now, by any measure, one of the most thrilling places in the New World to grow them.

title: Rosa Kruger and the Old Vine Project
dek: The viticulturist who crossed the Western Cape for two decades, catalogue in hand, fighting to save the vineyards that define South African wine.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Great-Granddaughter's Inheritance

Rosa Kruger is the great-great-granddaughter of Paul Kruger, the Boer statesman who served as President of the South African Republic from 1883 to 1900. She came to viticulture late, after a career in other fields, and when she did, she found her attention drawn not to the new vineyards being planted across the Western Cape but to the old ones being torn up. For most of the late twentieth century, old vines in South Africa were considered an economic liability: low-yielding, hard to harvest, often planted to unfashionable varieties like Chenin Blanc, Cinsaut, and Sémillon. The prevailing logic was to grub them up and replant with higher-yielding, more marketable vines.

Kruger saw something different. Working as a vineyard manager for premium clients across the Western Cape, she realised that the old vineyards — the bush vines that had been dry-farmed for sixty, seventy, even a hundred years — were producing fruit of a quality that no young vineyard could match. They were deeply rooted, naturally low-yielding, and adapted to their sites in ways that science could not replicate. They were, in her word, heritage. And they were disappearing.
A Project Becomes a Movement

In 2002, Kruger founded the Old Vine Project (OVP), a non-profit organisation dedicated to identifying, certifying, and protecting South Africa's heritage vineyards. The criteria are strict: a vineyard must be at least thirty-five years old to qualify for the Certified Heritage Vineyard seal. Kruger and her colleague André Morgenthal spent years driving the back roads of the Swartland, the Olifants River, the Breede River Valley, and Stellenbosch, mapping old parcels, talking to farmers, and building a registry of sites that the industry had largely forgotten.
These old vines are more than part of our history. They're part of our future. They produce wines that no young vine can.

The impact has been transformative. As of recent counts, the OVP encompasses more than 5,400 hectares of certified old vines across over 130 member producers, with more than 350 wines carrying the Certified Heritage seal. The seal — a small logo on a bottle's back label — has become a mark of quality and a selling point in export markets. Producers like Eben Sadie, Andrea Mullineux, Boekenhoutskloof, and Torben Maack of Alheit Vineyards have built their reputations on old-vine Chenin Blanc and other varieties, and they have the OVP to thank for the infrastructure that makes their sourcing possible.
Climate and the Old-Vine Future

In recent years, Kruger's work has taken on a new relevance. As climate change pushes temperatures up and water becomes scarcer across the Western Cape, the deep-rooted, drought-tolerant old vines have proven remarkably resilient. They suffer less in heatwaves, recover faster from drought, and maintain acidity and structure in vintages where younger vineyards struggle. The vineyards that the industry once dismissed as obsolete may turn out to be its best insurance against a warming future.

Kruger is now in her seventies, and the Old Vine Project has outgrown any single person. But the movement she started — the patient, unglamorous work of cataloguing, certifying, and defending the Cape's oldest vineyards — has changed South African wine at its roots. Every bottle of old-vine Chenin Blanc, every single-vineyard Cinsaut, every heritage-certified red blend on a wine list somewhere in the world is, in part, her legacy.

title: Thandi: Empowerment Through Wine
dek: The story of South Africa's first agricultural Black Economic Empowerment project — where 250 farm worker families became majority owners of their own wine brand.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: An Industry Built on Exclusion

For most of its history, the South African wine industry operated on a simple division of labour: black hands in the vineyards, white faces in the cellars and boardrooms. The legacy of apartheid, layered on top of three centuries of colonial land dispossession, meant that by the time democracy arrived in 1994, almost no commercial wine farm in the country was owned by black South Africans. The wine on the shelf was grown and picked by people who, in most cases, could not afford to drink it and had no stake in the brand it carried.

The post-apartheid government's answer, in part, was Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) — a policy framework designed to increase black ownership and participation across the economy. In the wine industry, BEE produced a handful of high-profile experiments. The most significant early one was Thandi.
250 Families, 51 Percent

Thandi — the word means 'beloved' or 'loved one' in Xhosa — was launched in the late 1990s and early 2000s as the first agricultural BEE project in South Africa. The structure was radical for its time: 250 farm worker families, drawn from several wine farms in the Western Cape, were given a 51 percent majority stake in a wine brand of their own. The remaining equity was held by industry partners and investors who provided capital, winemaking expertise, and market access.

The model was not without its challenges. Academic studies of Thandi and similar projects — including work by Stefano Ponte and Andries du Toit — have noted that empowerment in the wine industry has often been partial, with black shareholders holding equity without full operational control, and with farm workers' own voices frequently absent from the narrative of transformation. The wine industry is capital-intensive, slow to generate returns, and deeply tied to land ownership, which makes genuine redistribution difficult. But Thandi represented something genuinely new: a wine that the people who made it could also call their own.
We are not just workers anymore. We are owners. That changes everything — how you see the vineyard, how you see the wine, how you see yourself.
A Model, and Its Limits

Thandi produces a range of wines — Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir — sourced from vineyards in the Elgin and Stellenbosch regions. The wines have been Fairtrade certified, and the brand has built a market in Europe, particularly in the UK and Scandinavia, where ethical sourcing carries real commercial weight. For the families involved, the dividends — while modest by the standards of the broader industry — have funded education, housing, and community projects.

Thandi is not the whole story of transformation in South African wine. As of recent counts, roughly 67 wine brands are black-owned, out of many hundreds — a small fraction of the total. Projects like Visio Vintners (launched in 2018, 51 percent owned by 40 black workers) have followed the Thandi template, and the number is growing. But the deeper questions — about land, about who profits, about who gets to be called a winemaker — remain unresolved. Thandi's significance is that it asked those questions first, and it answered them, however imperfectly, with a bottle.

title: 350 Years of Constantia Wine
dek: The oldest wine region in the Southern Hemisphere — where vines planted in 1685 still produce some of the world's most extraordinary bottles.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: The Cradle

The Constantia valley, a fifteen-minute drive from the centre of Cape Town, is the cradle of South African wine. It is also, by a comfortable margin, the oldest wine-producing region in the Southern Hemisphere. The story begins in 1685, when Simon van der Stel, Governor of the Cape Colony under the Dutch East India Company, was granted a tract of land on the lower slopes of Table Mountain and planted the first vines. He called the farm Constantia.

Van der Stel chose the site with care. The Constantia valley benefits from a unique combination of conditions: close proximity to the cold Atlantic Ocean, cooling south-easterly winds that funnel off the sea and through the valley, and ancient decomposed granite soils that drain rapidly and force the vines to root deeply. It is, by any measure, one of the coolest wine-growing pockets in South Africa. Van der Stel, who had trained in Europe, recognised it immediately.
The Sweet Wine That Conquered Europe

Within a few generations of Van der Stel's plantings, Constantia was producing one of the most famous wines in the world. The sweet, unfortified wines made from Muscat grapes — later known collectively as Constantia wine, and in their most refined form as Vin de Constance — became the luxury sweet wine of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They were drunk by European royalty, praised by Jane Austen and Charles Baudelaire, and requested by Napoleon on his deathbed. For over a century, Constantia was the only South African wine that the international market knew or cared about.

Then came phylloxera, the root louse that devastated European and South African vineyards alike in the late nineteenth century. The Constantia estates were hit hard. The original farm was subdivided into several smaller properties — Groot Constantia, Klein Constantia, Constantia Uitsig, Buitenverwachting, Steenberg, and others — many of which fell into disuse or were replanted to bulk varieties. The great sweet wine of the eighteenth century effectively vanished for a hundred years.
The Modern Valley

The revival began in the 1980s, when Klein Constantia undertook the painstaking work of recreating Vin de Constance from original cuttings and historical records. The first vintage of the revived wine was 1986. Around the same time, the other Constantia estates began to focus on quality: Groot Constantia, now South Africa's oldest operating wine farm at over 330 years old, leaned into its heritage; Steenberg, the oldest wine-producing farm in the valley, established a reputation for Sauvignon Blanc; Constantia Uitsig and Buitenverwachting built followings for their white and Bordeaux-style red wines.

Today, the Constantia Wine Route — the smallest of South Africa's official wine routes — comprises ten estates clustered in a narrow valley within sight of Table Mountain's eastern flank. The wines that define the modern valley are dry Sauvignon Blancs of exceptional finesse, Bordeaux-style reds, and, of course, the revived Vin de Constance. The cool climate that Van der Stel identified in 1685 still shapes every bottle. And Groot Constantia, the original farm, remains one of the oldest continuously operating wine brands in the world — a title that places a small valley in the Cape alongside the great estates of Europe in the small, patient business of making wine across centuries.

title: Boekenhoutskloof and the Semillon Revival
dek: A Franschhoek winery that bet on a forgotten white grape — and built one of South Africa's most celebrated old-vine wines from vines planted in 1902.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Grape Nobody Wanted

Semillon is not a fashionable grape in South Africa. For most of the late twentieth century, it was planted in declining quantities, often blended anonymously into white blends, or grubbed up entirely in favour of Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc. The variety, which makes some of the greatest white wines of Bordeaux and the Hunter Valley, had fallen out of favour. Old vineyards were disappearing. Then Boekenhoutskloof, the Franschhoek estate that Marc Kent built into one of South Africa's most recognisable brands, decided to look backwards.

The Franschhoek valley, tucked into the mountains east of Stellenbosch, contains a scattering of very old Semillon vineyards planted by farmers who, a century ago, had no idea their vines would one day be considered national treasures. Boekenhoutskloof identified three parcels — planted in 1902, 1936, and 1942 — and began working with them under the Certified Heritage Vineyard programme of the Old Vine Project. The oldest of the three, the 1902 block, is among the oldest recorded Semillon plantings in the country.
From Forgotten Vines to a Benchmark White

The Boekenhoutskloof Semillon, first released as a single-vineyard wine in the early 2000s, is sourced from those three old parcels. The 1902 vineyard sits on alluvial soils with a high stone content; the later plantings add complementary textures. The grapes are whole-cluster pressed, fermented in a mix of old oak and stainless steel, and aged on their lees for extended periods. The result is a white wine of unusual weight and texture — full-bodied, with notes of nectarine, tangerine, persimmon, honey, wax, and lanolin, held in tension by a flinty, saline acidity.
These vines were planted before anyone alive was born. They have seen two world wars, the end of apartheid, and the rebirth of South African wine. They make a wine that carries all of that.

The wine has become a reference point for what South African Semillon can be. The 2021 vintage was featured in James Suckling's Top 100 Wines of South Africa, and vertical tastings of the wine across multiple vintages — most notably a comprehensive tasting published by Wine Anorak — have shown that it ages gracefully for a decade or more, developing layers of honey, dried apricot, and beeswax without losing its structural spine.
A Revival Beyond One Estate

Boekenhoutskloof's commitment to old-vine Semillon has helped spark a broader revival. Other producers — among them Mullineux, Sadie Family, and Alheit Vineyards — have begun working with the variety, sourcing fruit from heritage parcels across the Swartland and Franschhoek. The Old Vine Project's certification work has made it easier to identify and protect these vineyards, and the market for textured, ageworthy white wines has grown alongside them.

What the Boekenhoutskloof Semillon proves is something South African wine is still learning to say out loud: that the country's oldest vineyards are not just historical curiosities but active resources, capable of producing wines that rank with the world's best whites. The vines planted in 1902 have outlived everyone who planted them. The wine they produce, vintage after vintage, is the argument that they should be allowed to keep going.

title: Carmen Stevens: Breaking Every Barrier
dek: The woman who graduated as South Africa's first black winemaker in 1995 — and three decades later, opened the country's first 100 percent black- and woman-owned winery.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Childhood Dream

Carmen Stevens grew up on the Cape Flats, the sandy expanse east of Cape Town where non-white South Africans were forcibly relocated under apartheid. Wine was not part of her childhood. What she had was a fascination — fed, she has said, by glimpses of a world that seemed impossibly distant — with how grapes could become something that people travelled across the world to taste. It was a childhood dream that, in the South Africa of the 1980s, should have been impossible for a young woman of colour to pursue.

She pursued it anyway. In 1995, Stevens graduated as the first black person — and the first person of colour — to study winemaking at Stellenbosch University and qualify as a winemaker in South Africa. The year mattered. It was one year after the end of apartheid, one year after Nelson Mandela became president. The wine industry, like every other institution in the country, was being forced to open itself to people it had spent three centuries excluding. Stevens walked through the door and did not look back.
A Decade in Other People's Cellars

For the next decade and a half, Stevens worked as a winemaker for established estates, learning the craft in other people's cellars. The work was demanding, and the environment, in the early years, was often unwelcoming. She has spoken about the isolation of being the only black woman in tasting rooms, in industry meetings, in technical forums — the constant, low-grade implication that she did not quite belong. She responded, as she has put it, by outworking everyone around her.
I had to be twice as good to be taken half as seriously. So I became twice as good. It was the only answer I could give.

In 2011, Stevens launched her own label, Carmen Stevens Wines, with backing from Naked Wines, the crowd-funded wine platform that connected her directly with thousands of international subscribers. The arrangement gave her something she could not have found through traditional South African channels: capital, a guaranteed market, and the freedom to make wine entirely on her own terms. She produced Chenin Blanc, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, and other varieties, drawing fruit from across the Western Cape.
The First of Its Kind

Then, in 2019, Stevens registered the first 100 percent black- and woman-owned winery in Stellenbosch — and, as far as the records show, in South Africa. The distinction matters. BEE projects, joint ventures, and empowerment brands have existed in the industry for two decades, but they have almost always involved white partners holding equity and exercising control. Stevens's winery is entirely her own: owned, operated, and run by a black woman, on terms that she set.

Her wines have earned top international awards, and she has been named South Africa's Entrepreneur of the Year. She has been profiled by Deutsche Welle, featured in industry magazines across Europe and the United States, and held up — alongside Ntsiki Biyela — as the face of a changing industry. But the work, as Stevens is the first to acknowledge, is far from done. The cellar floor is more diverse than it was in 1995, but the boardroom is not. The land is still overwhelmingly white-owned. The story Carmen Stevens tells, in every bottle and every interview, is that transformation is not an event but a long, unfinished argument — and she intends to keep winning it.

title: KWV and the Transformation of South African Wine
dek: The cooperative founded in 1918 that controlled the Cape wine industry for seventy years — and the forces that finally broke its grip.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Cooperative Born in Crisis

On 8 January 1918 — the same year Nelson Mandela was born — a group of wine farmers in the Western Cape gathered in Paarl to sign a document that would shape South African wine for the next seven decades. They called their new organisation the Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging van Zuid-Afrika, the Cooperative Winemakers' Association of South Africa. Its first chairman was Dr. Charles Kohler. Its purpose was simple: to save an industry that was collapsing.

The Cape wine industry at the end of the First World War was in crisis. Overproduction had driven prices through the floor. Farmers were uprooting vineyards or pouring wine away. The new cooperative, with the backing of the government, was empowered to fix minimum prices, control surplus production through distillation quotas, and regulate exports. Within a few years, KWV had become the most powerful institution in South African wine — and it would remain so for the rest of the twentieth century.
The Monopoly Years

For the next seventy years, KWV functioned as a quasi-state body with near-monopoly control over the South African wine industry. It determined what farmers could plant, how much they could sell, and at what price. It ran the distilleries that converted surplus wine into brandy. It controlled the export market. And, crucially, it enforced a system that rewarded volume over quality: farmers were paid by the tonne, not by the character of the fruit, and the incentive structure pushed the industry toward bulk production and away from fine wine.

The system was efficient in its way. It stabilised an industry that had been lurching from crisis to crisis, and it made KWV one of the largest wine and spirits organisations in the world. But the cost was high. South African wine, for most of the KWV era, was associated internationally with cheap brandy, fortified wine, and undistinguished bulk reds and whites. The country's old vineyards, its diverse terroirs, and its small producers were systematically marginalised in favour of industrial-scale output. And the industry was, like every other institution in apartheid South Africa, organised along racial lines: black workers in the vineyards, white farmers and cooperative officials in charge.
The End of the Quota

The break came in the early 1990s. As apartheid ended and international sanctions lifted, the South African wine industry was suddenly exposed to global competition it had been shielded from for decades. The KWV's monopoly — which depended on a closed domestic market — became untenable. In 1992, the quota system was abolished. Farmers were free to plant what they wanted, sell to whom they wanted, and set their own prices. In 1997, KWV was converted from a cooperative into a private company, and its regulatory powers were stripped away.

The transformation was painful and uneven. Many farmers who had grown up under the KWV system had no idea how to compete in a market that rewarded quality. But the opening also unleashed the wave of innovation that would define the next three decades: the Swartland revolution, the old-vine movement, the rise of single-vineyard Chenin Blanc, the emergence of estates like Kanonkop, Boekenhoutskloof, Sadie Family, and Mullineux onto the international stage. None of it would have been possible under the old system. KWV, now a much-diminished commercial wine and spirits producer, still exists — a company that once ruled an industry, now competing within one. The cooperative that was founded to save South African wine ended up, for a time, holding it back. Its dismantlement was the condition for everything that has happened since.

title: The Cape's MCC Revolution
dek: How a Stellenbosch winemaker's 1969 trip to Champagne sparked a sparkling wine movement that now includes over 250 producers.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Trip to Champagne

In 1969, Frans Malan, the winemaker at Simonsig Wine Estate in Stellenbosch, travelled to Champagne. He went as a curious visitor. He came back as a man with a mission. The traditional method of making sparkling wine — primary fermentation in tank, followed by a second fermentation in the bottle, with extended ageing on the lees and hand riddling — had been refined in the chalk cellars of northern France for three centuries. Malan was convinced that the cool-climate slopes of Stellenbosch could produce the base wine it required.

The technical challenges were formidable. South Africa, in the late 1960s, had no tradition of quality sparkling wine production. The equipment for bottle fermentation, riddling, and disgorgement had to be imported or improvised. The grape varieties traditionally used in Champagne — Pinot Noir and Chardonnay — were not widely planted. And the regulatory environment, dominated by KWV, offered no framework for a new category. Malan pressed on regardless.
Kaapse Vonkel: The First Cape Sparkle

In 1971, Simonsig produced South Africa's first bottle-fermented sparkling wine. Two years later, in 1973, the estate released the first commercial vintage under the name Kaapse Vonkel — Afrikaans for 'Cape Sparkle.' It was the birth of a category. The wine was made in the traditional method, with the second fermentation taking place in the bottle, exactly as in Champagne, and it was aged on its lees for an extended period to develop the bready, autolytic complexity that defines the world's best sparkling wines.

Kaapse Vonkel was an instant success, and it became the catalyst for a movement. Other producers, seeing what Malan had done, began experimenting with bottle fermentation. The category needed a name. 'Champagne' was geographically protected and legally off-limits. 'Méthode Cap Classique' — 'Cap Classique Method' — was coined to describe South African sparkling wines made in the traditional method, and the term has since become a mark of quality recognised internationally.
I went to Champagne and I came back believing that the Cape could make wine with bubbles that were worth drinking. It took twenty years for everyone else to believe it too.
From One Wine to 250 Producers

Today, the Cap Classique category includes over 250 producers, making it one of the most dynamic sparkling wine movements in the Southern Hemisphere. The Cap Classique Association, founded to promote and regulate quality, has established standards for lees ageing (a minimum of twelve months, with many producers ageing far longer), grape variety, and production method. The best examples — from producers like Graham Beck, Méthode Cap Classique specialists like J.C. le Roux, and the Simonsig estate itself, now run by Frans Malan's grandson Michael — can stand alongside good Champagne in blind tastings.

What Frans Malan started in 1969 has become a defining feature of South African wine. Cap Classique is not an imitation of Champagne; it is a distinct expression of the Cape, made from grapes grown in South African soils, aged in South African cellars, and shaped by the particular cool-climate pockets of Stellenbosch, Elgin, and the Hemel-en-Aarde. It began with one winemaker who believed, against the evidence of his entire industry, that bubbles could be serious. The 250 producers who followed him are the proof that he was right.

title: Sadie Family Old Vine Series: A Love Letter in Eight Wines
dek: How Eben Sadie's single-vineyard Old Vine Series turned forgotten parcels into some of the most sought-after white wines in South Africa.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: Die Ouwingerdreeks

Alongside his flagship Columella and Palladius blends, Eben Sadie makes a series of single-vineyard wines called Die Ouwingerdreeks — the Old Vine Series. The project is, in its way, as defining as the blends that made his name. The series comprises eight wines, each sourced from a single old-vine parcel, each named for the site or the farmer who owns it. Together, they form a kind of love letter to the heritage vineyards of the Western Cape — and a practical argument for why they should be preserved.

The Old Vine Series began, like so much of Sadie's work, as an act of stubbornness. He had spent years driving the back roads of the Swartland, the Olifants River, and Stellenbosch, looking for old vines. What he found were vineyards that the industry had forgotten — parcels of Chenin Blanc, Palomino, Grenache Blanc, and Sémillon planted fifty, seventy, a hundred years ago, dry-farmed, never irrigated, tended by farmers who were, in many cases, the third or fourth generation of their families to work the land. The vines were struggling. Yields were tiny. The farmers were being offered next to nothing for their fruit. Sadie started buying.
Mev. Kirsten and the Oldest Chenin

The most celebrated wine in the series is Mev. Kirsten — Mrs. Kirsten — named for the woman whose family owns the vineyard. The parcel sits at the foot of Mount Bothmaskop in the Jonkershoek valley near Stellenbosch. The vines were planted between 1905 and 1920, making it, by widespread consensus, the oldest Chenin Blanc vineyard in South Africa. It is just over one hectare. In the first vintage, the vines were struggling so badly that Sadie was not sure he would have any wine at all.

The maiden vintage was 2006. Since then, Mev. Kirsten has become one of the most acclaimed white wines in the country. The 2024 vintage was rated 97 points by Robert Parker's Wine Advocate, a score almost unheard of for a South African white. The wine is fermented and aged in old oak foudres, with no new wood, no added acidity, and minimal intervention. The result is a Chenin Blanc of extraordinary depth and minerality — a wine that seems to carry the history of the vineyard in its texture.
Skurfberg: A Mountain on the West Coast

Another benchmark in the series is Skurfberg, sourced from old bush vines on the Skurfberg Mountain in the Citrusdal region of the Olifants River. The vines were planted between 1940 and 1955 on decomposed sandstone soils, unirrigated, clinging to rugged terrain that looks more like citrus country than vineyard. The grapes are whole-cluster pressed and aged in old foudres. The wine is powerful and mineral, with a chalky grip that has drawn comparisons to the great Chenins of the Loire.
These vineyards are a gift. They were planted by people who are dead, tended by people who are old, and drunk by people who don't know their names. My job is to make sure the wine remembers.

The Old Vine Series — which also includes wines like Kokerland, Radio Kata, and Pofadder — is not a commercial project in any conventional sense. Production of each wine is measured in hundreds of cases. The fruit is expensive relative to its yield. The winemaking is slow and labour-intensive. But the series has done more than almost any other project to establish the idea that South Africa's old vines are a national patrimony, worthy of being named, bottled, and remembered. Every wine in the series is a small act of preservation. Together, they are the closest thing the Cape has to a written record of its own viticultural past.

title: Porseleinberg: The Mountain That Became a Vineyard
dek: A single block of schist on a Swartland ridge — and the Syrah that turned an impossible site into one of South Africa's perfect scores.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Ridge of Schist

Porseleinberg — 'Porcelain Mountain' — is a ridge of schist in the Swartland, north of Wellington. For most of recorded history, it was considered too dry, too rocky, and too windswept for anything except grazing. The soil is a hard, laminated shale that breaks under the plough into shards. The rainfall is low. The summer heat is brutal. It is, by every conventional measure, the last place you would plant a vineyard.

But the same conditions that make Porseleinberg inhospitable also make it, for a certain kind of winemaker, irresistible. The schist forces the vines to root deeply. The wind keeps the canopy small and the crop light. The heat ripens the fruit fully, but the cool nights — the Swartland's secret weapon, with Atlantic breezes funneling inland every afternoon — preserve acidity. It is, in other words, a Syrah site. And in the early 2000s, that is exactly what it became.
A Single-Vineyard Syrah

The Porseleinberg Syrah, made under the Sadie Family umbrella, is a single-vineyard wine sourced entirely from the ridge. The vines are farmed without irrigation, planted at high density, and trained low to the ground to protect them from the wind. The winemaking is minimal: whole-cluster fermentation, gentle extraction, ageing in large old oak foudres. The goal, as with all of Eben Sadie's wines, is to let the site speak — and on Porseleinberg, the site has a great deal to say.

The wine is dark, structured, and savoury, with none of the sweetness or jamminess that plagues warm-climate Syrah. There is black fruit, pepper, and a pronounced mineral edge — the schist, tasters have noted for years, seems to translate directly into the wine's texture, giving it a grippy, almost crushed-rock character that no other South African Syrah quite matches. It is a wine built for the long term: the best vintages need a decade in bottle to reveal their full architecture.
Perfect Scores and a New Benchmark

The Porseleinberg Syrah has, in recent years, achieved something almost unprecedented in South African wine: perfect 100-point scores from major international critics. The 2015, 2018, and 2019 vintages — alongside the Kanonkop Paul Sauer and the Sadie Family Columella — were each awarded the maximum score, placing them in the rarefied company of the world's most celebrated red wines. It was, for a single vineyard on a ridge in the Swartland, a staggering recognition.
Porseleinberg is the most extreme site I work. The vines suffer. The yields are tiny. But the wine that comes off that schist is unlike anything else I have ever tasted.

The significance of Porseleinberg extends beyond the scores. It is proof — along with the Syrahs of Mullineux, Boekenhoutskloof, and others — that the Swartland can produce world-class expressions of the grape that defines the Northern Rhône. It is proof that South Africa's most unpromising landscapes can, in the right hands, yield its most extraordinary wines. And it is a reminder that the Swartland revolution, which began with Eben Sadie and eight thousand pounds, is still producing new chapters. The mountain that nobody wanted is now one of the most famous vineyard sites in the Southern Hemisphere.

title: Mev. Kirsten: The Oldest Chenin in the Country
dek: A one-hectare parcel of vines planted before the First World War — and the woman whose family has kept them alive for four generations.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: At the Foot of Bothmaskop

In the Jonkershoek valley, just outside Stellenbosch, at the foot of Mount Bothmaskop, there is a vineyard. It is small — just over one hectare, some accounts say closer to 0.7. It is planted to Chenin Blanc, the workhorse white grape of the Cape, in bush vine form, untrellised, sprawling. And it is old. The vines were planted between 1905 and 1920, which makes it, by widespread agreement, the oldest Chenin Blanc vineyard in South Africa. It belongs to a woman named Mrs. Kirsten — Mev. Kirsten, in Afrikaans — and her family.

To stand in the vineyard is to stand in a kind of living archive. The vines are gnarled, twisted, their trunks thick as a forearm. They are planted on a wonky spacing that predates mechanical harvesting, in soils of decomposed sandstone and alluvial granite that drain quickly and hold little water. There is no irrigation. There has never been. The vines have survived on rainfall alone for over a century, through droughts, floods, phylloxera scares, two world wars, the entire span of apartheid, and the democratic dispensation that followed. They are, in every meaningful sense, survivors.
Eben Sadie and the Maiden Vintage

Eben Sadie began working with the vineyard in the early 2000s, as part of his Old Vine Series. The first vintage of the Mev. Kirsten Chenin Blanc was 2006. In that first year, the vines were struggling so badly — the yields were infinitesimal, the fruit thin and stressed — that Sadie was not certain he would have any wine at all. He made just a few hundred bottles. They sold out immediately to a small circle of collectors and trade who recognised, almost at once, that something unusual was happening.

The wine is made with deliberate restraint. The grapes are whole-cluster pressed. The juice is fermented with native yeast in old oak foudres — large casks that impart no flavour of their own. There is no new oak, no added acidity, no skin contact, no tricks. The wine is aged on its lees for an extended period, then bottled, unfined and unfiltered, and released only when Sadie believes it is ready. The 2024 vintage was rated 97 points by Robert Parker's Wine Advocate, one of the highest scores ever given to a South African white wine.
That vineyard should not exist anymore. By every economic logic, it should have been grubbed up decades ago. It exists because one family refused to let it go.
Why Old Vines Matter

What makes the Mev. Kirsten vineyard — and the wine it produces — so significant is not just its age. It is what that age represents. Old vines, as Rosa Kruger and the Old Vine Project have spent two decades arguing, produce fruit that young vines cannot. Their root systems reach deep, accessing water and minerals that younger plants cannot touch. Their yields are naturally low, concentrating flavour. And they are, crucially, adapted to their sites in ways that no newly planted vineyard can be — they have spent a century learning how to grow in this particular patch of earth.

The Mev. Kirsten Chenin Blanc is the proof. It is a wine of extraordinary depth and minerality, with a texture that no young-vine Chenin can match. It is a wine that carries its history not as a marketing story but as a physical reality, in the glass. And it is, in the end, a tribute to the Kirsten family — to Mrs. Kirsten, to her parents and grandparents who planted the vines, and to the generations of hands that have tended them. The vineyard should not exist. It exists because someone decided it mattered. The wine, vintage after vintage, is the argument that they were right.

title: Bosman Family: Eight Generations on One Farm
dek: From a vine nursery in 1798 to one of the most sustainable estates in the Cape — the Bosman family has been growing vines in Wellington for over two centuries.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: The Bovlei and the Original Farm

The Bovlei is a narrow valley outside Wellington, about an hour's drive north-east of Cape Town, sheltered by the Limiet Mountains and watered by the Berg River. It is good vineyard country: warm enough to ripen reds, cooled by afternoon breezes, with well-drained soils. The Bosman family settled there in 1798, on a farm they called Lelienfontein. They have been there ever since.

Eight generations is a long time in any business. In wine, it is nearly unheard of. The Bosman family has farmed the same land in Wellington for over two centuries, through the colonial era, the Boer Wars, the union of South Africa, the rise and fall of apartheid, and the democratic dispensation. They have watched varieties come and go, markets open and close, and an entire industry transform itself around them. Through it all, they have kept growing vines.
From Wine to Nursery and Back

For most of the twentieth century, the Bosman family did not produce wine under their own label. They were vine growers — and, more specifically, vine nursery operators. In 1957, the family shifted their focus from wine production to the propagation of vine cuttings, known locally as stokkies. The Bosman nursery became one of the most important in South Africa, supplying certified, disease-free planting material to vineyards across the Western Cape and beyond. In an industry where the quality of the vine in the ground determines the quality of the wine in the bottle, the Bosmans, quietly, became foundational.

The return to estate wine production came in the early 2000s, under the eighth generation. The family began making wine from their own vineyards again, drawing on the genetic resources of the nursery and the deep knowledge of Wellington terroir that eight generations of farming had given them. The wines — Chenin Blanc, Pinotage, Cabernet Sauvignon, and others — were released under the Bosman Family Vineyards label, and they quickly drew notice for their quality and their sense of place.
Faith, Love, and Hope

The Bosman estate operates under a family motto of three words: Faith, Love, and Hope. It is, depending on your perspective, either a charming sentiment or a serious operational philosophy. In practice, it has meant something concrete. The Bosmans were early adopters of Fairtrade certification, and the estate runs a worker-ownership model that gives the people who work the vines a stake in the land they farm. They have invested heavily in sustainable viticulture, with the estate certified organic and biodynamic in recent years.
Eight generations teaches you patience. You do not farm for next year. You farm for the generation after you.

Today, Bosman Family Vineyards operates across two sites — the original Wellington estate in the Bovlei, and a second property near Hermanus on the cooler south coast. The Wellington estate remains the heart, with its historic homestead, its vine nursery, and its old vineyards, some of which are now certified under the Old Vine Project. The family's story — from 1798 to the present, through every convulsion of South African history — is a reminder that wine, at its best, is a multi-generational act of faith. The Bosmans have kept that faith for over two hundred years. The vines, vintage after vintage, are the evidence.

title: Aslina Wines: A Grandmother's Name on the World Stage
dek: How Ntsiki Biyela's own label — named for the grandmother who raised her — became an international ambassador for the new South African wine.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: Thirteen Years Before the Leap

Ntsiki Biyela spent thirteen years as a winemaker before she put her own name — or rather, her grandmother's name — on a bottle. It was a deliberate wait. She had become, in 2004, the first black woman to work as a winemaker in South Africa, at Stellekaya in Stellenbosch. She had learned the craft, earned medals, built a reputation. But she knew, from the beginning, that she wanted to make wine that was entirely her own — wine that carried not just her skill but her story.

In 2016, she left Stellekaya and founded Aslina Wines. The name was not chosen lightly. Aslina was Biyela's grandmother, a woman who raised her in Mahlabathini, a village in the hills of KwaZulu-Natal, and who embodied, in Biyela's telling, the strength and determination that she wanted the brand to carry. Every bottle of Aslina wine is, in a sense, a tribute — not to a famous winemaker or a historic estate, but to a grandmother in a rural village who never tasted wine but whose labor made everything that followed possible.
The Wines

Aslina produces a focused portfolio. The Sauvignon Blanc, sourced from Western Cape vineyards, is crisp and bright, with the tropical-fruit character that South African Sauvignon does so well. The Cabernet Sauvignon, drawn from Stellenbosch, is the flagship: a fruit-forward but structured wine with cassis, blackberry, and plum notes, aged in French oak, and built for the table. There is a Chardonnay, rounder and richer, and Umthunzi — a Bordeaux-style red blend whose name means 'in the shade of the tree' in Zulu, evoking the gathering places of Biyela's childhood.

The wines have been well received. The Cabernet Sauvignon has drawn strong reviews from Wine Enthusiast and other international publications. The Sauvignon Blanc has built a loyal following, particularly in the United States. And the brand has become, for a growing audience of international drinkers, an introduction not just to South African wine but to the changing face of who makes it.
My grandmother never drank wine. She never had the chance. But her strength is in every bottle. That is what Aslina means to me.
An Ambassador for Change

What sets Aslina apart from many empowerment-era brands is its independence. Biyela owns the company, sources her own fruit, and makes the wine. She is not a figurehead, not a joint-venture partner, not the black face on a white-owned label. Aslina is hers. That distinction — obvious in principle, rare in practice — has made her a sought-after voice in the international conversation about diversity in wine.

Biyela has been profiled by Forbes, interviewed by Grape Collective, featured in documentaries, and invited to speak at wine conferences across the world. She has used that platform to talk not just about her own wines but about the broader structural inequities of the South African industry: the concentration of land ownership, the slow pace of transformation, the thousands of black South Africans who work in wine country and have never been invited to taste what they help produce. Aslina, in her hands, is more than a brand. It is an argument — that the future of South African wine depends on opening its doors to the people its past excluded. The grandmother's name, on bottles from Stellenbosch to New York, is the proof that the argument can be won.

title: The Future of South African Wine: New Regions, New Faces
dek: From the cool slopes of Elim to the heights of the Cederberg — how climate change, a new generation, and a willingness to look sideways are reshaping the Cape.
author: Decanta Editorial

blocks.text: A Region Points the Way

In early 2025, James Suckling's South Africa tasting report carried a headline that would have been unimaginable two decades ago: 'Greatness Finds a Foothold: Swartland Points the Way for South African Wine.' The report, which awarded near-perfect scores to the 2023 Columella and Palladius, concluded that the Swartland — the dry, schist-and-granite country north of Cape Town that was, until recently, written off as bulk territory — was now the compass needle for the country's fine wine ambitions. It was a verdict less on a single vintage than on two decades of transformation.

The South African wine industry that has emerged from the shadow of KWV, apartheid, and international isolation is younger, more diverse, and more geographically scattered than the one that preceded it. The old certainties — that serious red wine came from Stellenbosch, that Constantia meant Sauvignon Blanc and dessert wine, that the industry was run by a handful of Afrikaner families — have given way to something messier, more interesting, and still very much in motion.
New Regions, Cooler Sites

The most visible change is geographic. As the Western Cape warms — the MDPI's 2025 climate analysis projects substantial temperature increases, decreased precipitation, and more extreme weather events across South African wine regions — producers are pushing into cooler, higher, and more marginal sites. Elim, at the southern tip of the continent near Cape Agulhas, is now producing Sauvignon Blancs and Syrahs of startling freshness from vineyards battered by Antarctic winds. The Cederberg, high in the mountains east of Citrusdal, is gaining a reputation for high-altitude whites. Plettenberg Bay, on the Garden Route, and the upper reaches of the Hemel-en-Aarde are being explored for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay that would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

The logic is simple: as the traditional Stellenbosch and Paarl regions heat up, the search for acidity, elegance, and freshness leads southward, upward, and toward the sea. Sommeliers in Cape Town and Johannesburg increasingly speak of these marginal, emerging regions as the Cape's answer to climate change. The old vineyards, too — the subject of Rosa Kruger's Old Vine Project — have proven unexpectedly resilient, their deep root systems and natural drought tolerance giving them an advantage in hotter, drier vintages.
New Faces

The other transformation is human. For three centuries, the South African wine industry was defined by its exclusions: black South Africans grew the grapes, picked the harvest, and staffed the cellars, but were systematically barred from ownership, education, and recognition. That is changing, slowly and unevenly. Ntsiki Biyela, Carmen Stevens, and a growing cohort of black winemakers — among them Malmesy Rangaka of M'hudi, the late Sidumo Mbobo, and a new generation of cellar assistants moving into winemaking roles — are reshaping what a South African winemaker is allowed to look like. Roughly 67 wine brands are now black-owned, a small fraction of the total but a doubling in a decade.
The future of South African wine is not in one region or one grape. It is in the people who are now, for the first time, allowed to make it.
What Comes Next

The challenges are real. Climate change is not theoretical in the Western Cape; the 2015-2018 drought, which brought Day Zero within sight of Cape Town, was a brutal warning. Land redistribution remains unresolved, and the pace of transformation is, by every honest assessment, too slow. The global market for premium wine is crowded, and South Africa, despite its quality, still fights for recognition against the established reputations of France, Italy, and California.

And yet. The 2025 harvest was strong across all ten wine regions. Wines of South Africa, the industry export body, launched a bold new campaign — 'There's Sunshine Inside' — positioning the country's wine around something more than climate. The South Africa Wine Summit, held in Stellenbosch, focused on sustainability, new territories, and innovation. The Swartland continues to point the way. The old vines continue to prove their worth. And a generation of winemakers who were children when apartheid ended are now, finally, making wine on their own terms. The future of South African wine is not guaranteed. But it has never been more interesting.
